# 2.0 Tutorial 2 — Exploring the Ocean from Space

![Tutorial 2 banner](Figs/banner.jpg)

*Figure 1: AI image generated by Canva*

**Keywords:** POC, chlorophyll-a, SST, SSHA

## What this tutorial is about

In this tutorial you will use satellite data to look at the ocean from several different angles.

You will work with:

- **Chlorophyll-a**, an indicator of how much phytoplankton is in the water
- **Particulate organic carbon (POC)**, the amount of carbon held in particles in the ocean
- **Sea surface temperature (SST)**, the temperature of the ocean surface
- **Sea surface height anomalies (SSHA)**, changes in sea surface height, which tell us about ocean circulation
- **Ocean surface currents**, how the water is actually moving

Each of these describes a different aspect of the ocean, but they are connected.

Temperature affects how easily the ocean mixes. Mixing controls how nutrients move up through the water column, and nutrients control how much phytoplankton can grow. Changes in circulation move warm and cold water from one region to another, which changes the temperature, and so changes the mixing again.

By the end of the tutorial you will use all five measurements together to investigate those links, and to describe what happens to them during the El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO).

## How this tutorial works

**Every cell runs as it stands.** You do not need to understand every line of Python, and you do not have to change anything to get the figures the assignment asks for. Each notebook introduces an idea, you run a cell and see it, then you change a setting and run it again. The point is not getting the code to run, it is understanding **why the result changed when you changed the setting** — so read the `Try changing these` block at the top of a cell, that is where the thinking is.

## Part A — Understand the satellites
Before working with satellite data, it helps to understand the satellite that produced it: where it is, how often it observes an area, and what it can and cannot see. These limitations explain many of the patterns you will see in your maps.
There are **9 mission questions**, grouped by satellite rather than by notebook: the four groups below are numbered 2.1 to 2.4 after their satellite, and the OSCAR group (2.4) is answered from notebook 2.3, part 2. **This handout and the answer template are the only places these questions appear**, the notebooks do not repeat them. For every question, **Where to find it** names the page or the notebook cell that has the answer, and **Write** lists at most two things to answer. The template has a placeholder under each one.

**One or two sentences per item is enough.** These are short questions. Part A is worth a small share of the marks, and a longer answer does not earn more of them; the analysis in Parts B and C is where the credit is.

**2.1 Mission question 1.** PACE flies a sun-synchronous orbit, 676.5 km up at an inclination of 98°, which makes it cross the equator at the same local time — about 13:00 — on every pass. Why does that help when you compare one month with another?
> **Where to find it**
> - Notebook 2.1 §1, on how chlorophyll-a is worked out from a **ratio of reflected sunlight**. That is the fact the answer turns on.
>
> **Write**
> 1. Why crossing at the same local time every day helps when you compare one month with another. Think about the angle of the sun, and about what would change in the measurement if that angle were different each time.

**2.1 Mission question 2.** What does the chlorophyll-a measurement represent, and what range of values do you see?
> **Where to find it**

> - Notebook 2.1 §3, third code cell, prints a `Units` line.
> - Notebook 2.1 §4, the global map: its colour bar shows the values you actually see.
>
> **Write**

> **Paste:** `chl_poc_sst_south_china_sea_202501_202504.png`, captioned `2.1 — chl_poc_sst_south_china_sea_202501_202504.png`; `chl_poc_sst_north_pacific_gyre_202501_202504.png`, captioned `2.1 — chl_poc_sst_north_pacific_gyre_202501_202504.png`.

**Question 3.** How does sea surface temperature affect chlorophyll-a and POC, and why is the relationship not the same in the two regions?
> **Where to find it**
> - The same figures and table as question 2, from notebook 2.1 §9.
> - Under each region the cell prints a change line: the SST change in °C and the chlorophyll-a and POC changes as percentages, from January to April.
> - Notebook 2.1 §9, *Two kinds of ocean*, explains what a subtropical gyre is and what makes a shelf sea different. Item 3 turns on that difference.

> **Rule.** Compare the direction chlorophyll-a moves with the direction SST moves. **Opposite** directions — one up, the other down — is a **negative** relationship. The **same** direction is **positive**. If chlorophyll-a changes by less than 20 % either way, call it **weak**, whichever way the temperature went.
>
> **Paste:** nothing for this question.
>
> **Write**
> 1. South China Sea: the SST change in °C, the chlorophyll-a and POC changes in %, and the word positive, negative or weak.
> 2. North Pacific gyre: the SST change in °C, the chlorophyll-a and POC changes in %, and the word positive, negative or weak.
>
> #### Question 3, item 3 — why do the two regions behave differently?
>
> **This is the main interpretation question of Tutorial 2, and it carries the most credit of any item in the assignment. Aim for about 150–250 words.**
>
> A warmer surface layer changes how much the surface mixes with the water below, and so how many nutrients reach the sunlit surface. Use that chain — **SST → stratification and mixing → nutrients → chlorophyll-a and POC** — and explain why it produces a strong response in one region and almost none in the other. Two things to bring in: how much each region's temperature actually changed, and how far each one is from a coast, a shelf or a river. *Two kinds of ocean* in §9 gives you both.

### Questions 4–7 — Following one ENSO cycle through four measurements

ENSO is a climate phenomenon driven by changes in wind conditions and sea surface temperature over the tropical Pacific. These four questions follow one chain across the tropical Pacific (30°S–30°N, 90°E–60°W) for three periods — **December 2022**, **December 2023** and **July 2024** — each a different phase of the cycle:

> **question 4:** which ENSO phase each period is in, from a published index →
> **question 5:** what the sea surface height does →
> **question 6:** what the surface currents do →
> **question 7:** what the sea surface temperature does

You settle the phase first, independently, and then ask whether three different satellite measurements tell the same story.

**Before you start**

1. Answer question 4 first. Notebook 2.2 §9 will not run until you have put its answer into it.
2. Run notebook 2.2 top to bottom, then notebook 2.3. **The only thing you have to fill in anywhere is 2.2 §9**, and neither notebook needs an account. Notebook 2.3 covers both sea surface height (part 1) and ocean currents (part 2).
3. There is no SWOT data for December 2022, so question 5 reads that period off the Sentinel-6 and Jason-3 map in notebook 2.3 §7 instead.

**Question 4.** Identify the ENSO phase of each of the three periods using a published index, and say what the sea surface temperature of the central and eastern equatorial Pacific does in that phase.
> **Where to find it**
> - The Oceanic Niño Index (ONI) table: <https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/analysis_monitoring/enso/oni/v6/>. Each row is a year and each column is a three-month season.
> - December 2022: row **2022**, column **NDJ**. December 2023: row **2023**, column **NDJ**. July 2024: row **2024**, column **JJA**.
> - ENSO background, for the third column: <https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/enso/>
>
> **Rule.** +0.5 or higher is **El Niño**. −0.5 or lower is **La Niña**. Anything in between is **Neutral**.
>
> **Paste:** nothing for this question.
>
> **Write** (The table, plus one line.)
> 1. Fill in the table: for each period, the phase, the ONI value you read, and one sentence saying what the sea surface temperature of the central and eastern equatorial Pacific does in that phase. The three periods are three different phases, so the third column ends up describing all three.
> 2. One line: *Index used: ONI, from* followed by the URL.
> 3. Then open notebook 2.2 §9 and set `LA_NINA`, `EL_NINO` and `NEUTRAL` to the three period keys `"202212"`, `"202312"` and `"202407"`, one key each, according to the table you have just filled in. The cell will not run until you do, and nothing from it is handed in — it is there so you can check your table against the data.
>
> | Period | ENSO phase | ONI value | What the central and eastern equatorial Pacific SST does in this phase |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | December 2022 | | | |
> | December 2023 | | | |
> | July 2024 | | | |

**Question 5.** Describe how SSHA changes across the tropical Pacific between the three periods. Which period shows the strongest eastward displacement of warm water, and how large is the change in sea surface height? What does that imply about the thermocline?
> **Where to find it**
> - Notebook 2.3 §6, run as it is. Under the profile it prints, for each file, `west box`, `east box` and `east minus west`, in metres. Use the `SWOT_SSHA_202312` and `SWOT_SSHA_202407` lines.
> - December 2022 has no SWOT data. Use the map in notebook 2.3 §7 instead, and read it over the **same two strips** the SWOT numbers use, so the three periods are comparable. Along the equator, look at **140°E–170°E** for the west and **150°W–90°W** for the east. **That map spans 0° to 360° across the bottom, so those two strips are 140 to 170 and 210 to 270.** The profile figure you paste in shades and labels the same two boxes.
>
>   **All you need from that map is a sign.** It is built from narrow satellite tracks on a rainbow colour scale and neighbouring dots disagree by several centimetres, so do not try to read a number off it. Say whether each strip is above zero, below zero or near it, and give the sign of east minus west that follows. That is a full answer.
>
> **Paste:** `ssha_equatorial_profile_eq2_1deg.png`, captioned `2.3 — ssha_equatorial_profile_eq2_1deg.png`; `ssha_diff_SWOT_SSHA_202407_minus_SWOT_SSHA_202312_1deg.png`, captioned `2.3 — ssha_diff_SWOT_SSHA_202407_minus_SWOT_SSHA_202312_1deg.png`. The second file is the map titled *for question 5*.
>
> **Write**
> 1. The east-minus-west number for each period: the printed value in metres for December 2023 and July 2024, and for December 2022 the **sign only**, from the §7 map. Say which period has the largest positive value, which is the period in which the most warm water has moved east.
> 2. That largest value converted to a thermocline change, with the rule 10 cm ≈ 30 m. Example: +0.20 m is 20 cm, so about 60 m.

**Question 6.** Using your OSCAR maps of the total surface currents, describe whether there is any relation between the currents and the SSHA pattern you described in question 5. Do the currents match what you would expect from the ENSO phase of each period?
> **Where to find it**
> - Notebook 2.3 §12, run as it is. It draws the three total-current maps, one per period, all on the same colour scale. OSCAR covers December 2022, so all three periods are there.
> - Notebook 2.3 §13, run as it is. It prints, for each period, `on the equator` with the eastward speed in m/s, averaged over 160°E–200°E and 2°S–2°N. Positive is eastward, negative is westward.
> - Your east-minus-west SSHA numbers from question 5, and your phase table from question 4.
>
> **Paste:** `currents_oscar_currents_nrt_20231201.png`, captioned `2.3 — currents_oscar_currents_nrt_20231201.png`. That is the December 2023 map, the one period where the equatorial flow reverses. Look at all three in the notebook, but paste only this one.
>

Unlike questions 1 to 7, this one has no settled answer in the published record: **how does the El Niño happening now compare with the last strong one?** You answer it from sea surface height alone, against December 2023, the peak of the 2023–24 event.
